description: We are a team of motivated students and tech enthusiasts participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our team has experience in software development, AI/ML, data analysis, UI/UX, and problem-solving. We are looking for creative and collaborative members with skills in data science, GIS, space science, development, research, or media.
summary:
Earth's Hidden Signals is a free website that tells anyone whether the climate in their own town is really changing, or just varying by chance. Type any town on Earth to see what has changed there since 1981, what NASA projections say for 2041–2060, disasters recorded nearby and what to prepare for. A world heat map shows where warming is real, and other views show disaster hotspots, the year before past disasters, and NASA satellite maps.

For the challenge, we built a trend detective on NASA data: GISTEMP temperature, GPCP rainfall and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections, plus GDACS and NASA's Global Landslide Catalog for disasters. Every trend is tested with a corrected Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope, with false-discovery control, and checked against an independent record (CRU TS). Since 1981, 3,848 land areas have clearly warmed.

This matters because climate data usually ends as charts few people can read or trust. We turn it into plain answers in English and Bangla, so farmers, students and planners, starting in Bangladesh, can see what's coming and prepare. When a change is not yet clear, the site says so.
details:
What it does

Earth's Hidden Signals answers one question for any place on Earth: is the climate here really changing, or is it chance? Type a town and you get a one-page report:

- what changed since 1981 (temperature and rainy-season rain), with its own warming stripes;

- what NASA projections say for 2041–2060, on a middle-road and a high-emissions path, including very hot days a year;

- floods, cyclones, droughts and landslides recorded within 300 km since 2000;

- "signals together": months that were hot and dry, or very wet on wet ground, at once;

- what to prepare for, a climate twin somewhere else on Earth, and a card to download and share.

The site also has a world heat map of tested warming, disaster hotspots, "the year before a disaster" timelines, and NASA satellite maps.

How it works

A Python pipeline reads NASA GISTEMP v4 (temperature), GPCP v2.3 (rainfall) and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 (projections, six models), plus GDACS alerts and NASA's Global Landslide Catalog. Sen's slope measures how fast each place changes. A Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation, with false-discovery control across the map, decides whether the change is real. We repeated the main trends on an independent record (CRU TS) and they agree. The results are saved as data files, so the website is fast and free to use, with no login.

Benefits and impact

Climate data usually ends as charts that few people can read or trust. We give plain, tested answers in English and Bangla, so farmers, students and planners, starting in Bangladesh, can see what's coming and prepare. Next: daily rain and river data, a town report in every school, and partners in Bangladesh's disaster agencies.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, scikit-learn, netCDF4, shapely); TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS and Leaflet for the website, hosted on Vercel; Remotion for the demo videos. No special hardware.

What makes it creative

Every town gets its own warming stripes and a "climate twin" with the same change, half a world away. The "year before a disaster" view shows the heat and rain that came first.

What we considered

Honesty first. We dropped NASA POWER rainfall after finding sudden jumps in it. Our own AI test could not predict disaster years, so we never sell forecasts. When a change is not clear yet, the site says so. Disaster records are incomplete, and we label them that way. We kept the words few and offered Bangla so more people can use it.
